newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Iraq and U.N. lodge complaints on oil-for-food plan.
newsitem.headline: Iraq and U.N. lodge complaints on oil-for-food plan.

text.p: Iraq on Tuesday complained that food supplies under an "oil-for-food" plan were taking too long to arrive while U.N. sources said Baghdad was hindering operations on the ground.

After seeing Secretary-General Kofi Annan late on Monday Iraq's U.N. envoy Nizar Hamdoon appealed to non-aligned members of the Security Council on Tuesday to support his demand for speedier delivery of food supplies.
In response, U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard said Annan had promised to give Iraq more details on the deliveries and asked Hamdoon to relay "operational" matters to Baghdad.

The operational issues, according to the U.N. sources, included getting permission to use the airport in Baghdad rather than drive goods and personnel in from Jordan, allowing U.N. monitors to have their own communications and letting them move around freely without a government escort.

At issue is an "oil-for-food" agreement that took effect on Dec. 10 and permits Baghdad to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy food, medicine and other necessities to offset the effects of sanctions imposed after Iraq's August 1990 invasion of Kuwait. The United Nations was sending 155 monitors to Iraq to ensure equitable distribution of the humanitarian supplies.
Hamdoon said no food supplies had reached Iraq. He said the Security Council's sanctions committee was slow in approving them and U.N. procedures in general were "very cumbersome and time-consuming."

Taking up Iraq's complaint, Russia asked U.N. officials to give the Security Council a briefing this week on precisely what food supplies were in the pipeline and when they would reach Iraq, diplomats said.

Eckhard said oil sales had reached $386 million but only $113 million had been dispersed. Four contracts for foodstuffs were approved: $21 million for French wheat, $50 million for Australian wheat, $21 million for Thai rice and $5.5 million for tea from Jordan.

The sanctions commitee considered 10 applications, blocked one and put five others on hold, he said. But he said the United Nations had received 131 applications from vendors selling food, medicine and other goods and U.N. staff passed the applications to the sanctions committee depending on the funds available from oil revenues.

Hamdoon told reporters on Monday he asked Annan to let Baghdad know why contracts were rejected so Iraq could make sure technical matters were resolved. He said Iraq also wanted to decide which contracts should be substituted in place of those rejected.
